D1p1: About 110,000 households in Hong Kong live in subdivided units (SDUs).
SDUs are flats carved into small cubicles, often with shared kitchens and bathrooms.
Median SDU rent is roughly 30 percent below mainstream private flats.
On a per-square-foot basis SDU tenants pay a premium of 15 to 25 percent.
D1p2: SDU tenants are disproportionately new arrivals, single-parent households and residents waiting for public housing.
The average waiting time for public housing has hovered around five and a half years.
For these households the SDU is not a choice but a residual option while the queue moves.
D1p3: Policy debate has long centred on whether to regulate rents in this segment.
Hong Kong operates the Tenancy Control Ordinance of 2021.
The Tenancy Control Ordinance of 2021 capped rent increases within an existing tenancy but did not cap the initial rent level.
The Tenancy Control Ordinance of 2021 excluded SDUs with co-living services from key provisions.
D1p4: Tightening raises the classic question of rent economics.
The question is whether capping the initial rent helps tenants or shrinks the stock they depend on.
The answer depends on supply elasticity.
The answer depends on enforcement capacity.
The answer depends on what happens to households if units exit the market.
D2p1: Estimated SDU stock in 2019 was 100,800 units.
D2p2: Median SDU rent per square foot rose 6.8 percent in 2019-2021.
Median SDU rent per square foot rose 3.1 percent in 2021-2023 under the ordinance.
General private rent growth was 2.4 percent in 2019-2021.
General private rent growth was 1.7 percent in 2021-2023.
D2p3: Post-2023 figures rely on survey extrapolation.
Reporting of new tenancy terms is voluntary below the ordinance threshold.
D3p1: Mr Chan is a delivery driver.
Mr Chan lives with his wife and two children in a 120 sq ft cubicle.
Mr Chan moved in after a factory injury.
D3p2: He is split on the proposed tightening.
A hard cap would free maybe 800 dollars a month.
800 dollars a month is food for a month.
He fears landlords would rather convert cubicles back to storage rooms than deal with regulated tenants.
He has seen two units on his floor emptied and locked for a year.
D3p3: He does not name rent when asked what would help most.
The queue is five and a half years.
If the queue were three years instead of five and a half, he would accept any rent to leave.
D4p1: Mrs Wong is 67 years old and retired.
Mrs Wong has lived in an SDU for nine years and pays 4,200 dollars.
Mrs Wong's tenancy predates the 2021 ordinance.
Mrs Wong has never received a written tenancy agreement.
D4p2: She supports a hard cap on initial rents.
Her building has four SDU landlords.
She says none of the four SDU landlords would leave the business.
D4p3: Interviewers note a contradiction she does not see.
She reports two flats in her stairwell converted to non-residential storage after the ordinance.
She still believes landlords cannot exit.
D5p1: The Association represents owners of roughly 18,000 SDU units.
The Association argues a hard initial-rent cap is confiscatory.
Many owners hold thin margins after mortgage payments and rates.
Many owners faced 2021 compliance costs of windows, wiring and fire doors.
D5p2: Members will exit the segment if returns fall below mortgage cost.
Every unit converted back removes housing.
The removed housing, however poor, houses someone tonight.
D5p3: The Association concedes it has no data on members' actual margins.
The Association's compliance-cost figures cite a 2022 survey.
The survey had a 34 percent response rate and was self-reported.
D6p1: Standard theory predicts supply contraction under binding rent ceilings.
The elasticity is an empirical question.
In marginal stock, the long-run elasticity of SDU-type supply to controlled rent levels is estimated at 0.31 to 0.48 in the reviewed literature.
A 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years.
D6p2: The paper distinguishes first-generation controls (hard caps on levels) from second-generation controls (caps on increases within tenancies).
First-generation controls show consistent contraction effects.
Second-generation controls show small or null effects on stock.
The 2021 Hong Kong ordinance is second-generation, which explains the stable stock in the D2 index.
D6p3: Contraction removes units at the bottom.
The households that lose units are the same population the cap intends to protect.
Whether tenants gain depends on how many stay long enough in regulated tenancies to offset entrants who can no longer find units.
D6p4: The paper models a tightened cap scenario for a Hong Kong-like market.
A 15 percent cut in initial rents yields a net transfer of about 900 dollars per month to incumbents.
3,000 to 4,000 households per year are unable to enter the segment.
The households unable to enter are mostly new arrivals and newly formed households.
D7p1: Berlin capped rents on ~1.5 million flats at 2020.
Reported initial-offer rents for new listings fell sharply.
Classified-listing supply contracted measurably within a year.
Owners withheld or rerouted flats to non-controlled segments.
D7p2: The constitutional court struck the law down in 2021.
The court struck the law down on federal-competence grounds, not economic ones.
When the law fell, a backlog of suppressed increases released into the market.
Rents for new contracts jumped above the pre-cap trend line.
D7p3: Caps bind differently on new entrants than incumbents.
The tenants the cap protects are those already inside.
The bill is handed to those still outside.
D8p1: New York has regulated rents since 1947.
New York's rent regulation currently covers roughly 44 percent of rental stock.
New York's rent regulation is a second-generation scheme.
Increases are capped within tenancies, initial rents and vacancy are lightly regulated, and vacancy decontrol ended in 2019.
D8p2: Studies find stabilised units show lower mobility.
Tenants in stabilised units stay longer.
Measured rent gaps to unregulated units are wide.
Stock contraction is modest because the scheme is light at first-rent, the exact point Hong Kong's 2021 ordinance also left untouched.
D8p3: Maintenance incentives fall with regulated returns.
The 2019 tightening is associated with a measurable fall in available stabilised listings.
Owners shift units to other uses.
D9p1: A hard cap on initial SDU rents would almost certainly attract compensation claims under the Basic Law's protection of property rights if framed as a deprivation of rental income stream.
A cap framed as contractual-term regulation, like the 2021 ordinance, sits on firmer ground.
A cap framed as contractual-term regulation leaves the initial rent unregulated.
The initial rent is the actual pain point.
D9p2: Counsel assesses a middle instrument that caps initial rent by reference to a published per-square-foot band.
The band is indexed and reviewable.
Regulators can defend the instrument as rate-capping rather than confiscation.
Bands would need a survey infrastructure that does not currently exist.
D9p3: The government should expect judicial review from institutional owners without compensation.
The Association's submission (D5) previews the argument.
Litigation timeline alone would outlast a Council term.
D10p1: Current SDU inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year.
A band-based initial-rent cap requires a certifiable tenancy register.
The Rating and Valuation Department estimates 40 to 60 staff-years to stand up the register.
Members were briefed that a tightened cap is only as real as its inspection regime.
D10p2: The subcommittee's modelling note records a risk the public consultation omits.
The risk is that landlords reprice above-band initial rents.
The first instrument tenants hold is complaint.
Tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement or the newest arrivals.
D10p3: A member noted that the subcommittee could not identify any enforcement design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last.
The chair agreed to strike the member's statement from the public version.
The newest-arrival tail is the population named in D1.
D11p1: 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for a three-year security of tenure.
74 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for a faster public-housing offer.
Tenants name queue length and tenancy insecurity, not rent level, as the binding constraint.
D11p2: Rent caps treat the price symptom of a quantity problem.
The segment is tight because the queue is long.
Every unit of enforcement capacity spent policing rents is a unit not spent on inspection of conditions.
Harm is documented and immediate in inspection of conditions such as fire, partition, and ventilation.
D11p3: The report supports a narrow tightening.
The narrow tightening includes tenure security plus a light band on initial rents.
The report opposes a hard cap.
The report's positions are based on D6-type contraction arithmetic and its own survey's revealed preference.
D12p1: The Chief Executive's policy agenda names SDU regulation among housing priorities.
A consultation document is expected to float a 'floor-standard + rent band' package rather than a hard cap.
The consultation document cites Berlin's void order (D7) as a cautionary tale.
D12p2: Two think-tank pieces this spring argued opposite directions.
One piece cites the stable stock under the 2021 ordinance (D2) to argue capacity exists for more control.
The other piece cites D6's elasticity band to argue the visible stability is an artifact of a non-binding instrument.
The other piece argues a binding instrument behaves differently.
D12p3: Property shares moved little on the agenda news.
Analysts note listed developers hold little SDU exposure.
SDU exposure sits with small individual owners.
The small individual owners are the constituency D5 speaks for.
